```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.8, dpi = 110
)
logger::log_threshold(logger::WARN, namespace = "pdmS7")
pal <- c("#236b83", "#a26421", "#5b8c3a", "#8a3b6b", "#444444", "#b23b3b", "#9aa7b0")
```

Calibrating one catchment is careful, hands-on work. Calibrating sixty is a different job:
every catchment must be treated the same way, the run will take hours, something will go
wrong part way through, and the results only mean something when looked at together.
`calibrate_batch()` does that job. This article shows how to use it, step by step, and how to
read what comes out.

The example runs live on eight made-up catchments. Because we made them up, we know the
"true" parameter values, so at the end we can check how close calibration got. A real
batch works the same way, only bigger.

# What you need: one folder per catchment

Put each catchment in its own folder, named after it, inside one parent folder. Each folder
holds three files:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `forcing.csv` | Columns `time`, `rain` and `pet`: rainfall and potential evaporation in mm per time step |
| `flow.csv` | Column `q_m3s`: the measured river flow, one row per time step; gaps can be left empty |
| `basin.yml` | A few lines describing the catchment |

Here we build eight such folders. One of them, B06, has a fault, as real collections often
do: a stretch of negative evaporation from a corrupted file.

```{r folders}
basins <- file.path(tempdir(), "basins")
set.seed(2024)
n <- 24 * 60
time <- seq(as.POSIXct("2023-10-01", tz = "UTC"), by = 3600, length.out = n)
truths <- list()
for (i in 1:8) {
  id <- sprintf("B%02d", i)
  folder <- file.path(basins, id)
  dir.create(folder, recursive = TRUE)
  wet <- stats::runif(1, 0.04, 0.09)
  forcing <- data.frame(
    time = format(time, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
    rain = ifelse(stats::runif(n) < wet, stats::rgamma(n, 0.7, scale = stats::runif(1, 2, 4)), 0),
    pet = round(stats::runif(1, 0.04, 0.09), 3)
  )
  truth <- pdm_presets("standard")
  truth$area_km2 <- round(stats::runif(1, 10, 200))
  truth$fc <- stats::runif(1, 0.9, 1.2)
  truth$distribution$cmax <- stats::runif(1, 80, 250)
  truth$recharge$kg <- exp(stats::runif(1, log(20), log(300)))
  k <- sort(stats::runif(2, 1, 12))
  truth$surface$k1 <- k[1]
  truth$surface$k2 <- k[2]
  truths[[id]] <- truth
  flow <- run_pdm(pdm_from_config(truth), forcing[, c("rain", "pet")])$output$q_m3s *
    exp(stats::rnorm(n, 0, 0.04))
  if (id == "B06") forcing$pet[100:110] <- -0.05
  data.table::fwrite(forcing, file.path(folder, "forcing.csv"))
  data.table::fwrite(data.frame(q_m3s = flow), file.path(folder, "flow.csv"))
  writeLines(c(
    paste("catchment:", paste("Example", id)),
    paste("gauge:", id),
    paste("area_km2:", truth$area_km2),
    "calibration: [2023-10-11, 2023-11-14]",
    "validation: [2023-11-15, 2023-11-29]"
  ), file.path(folder, "basin.yml"))
}
list.files(basins)
```

A `basin.yml` is short. Only the area and the calibration period are required:

```{r yml}
cat(readLines(file.path(basins, "B01", "basin.yml")), sep = "\n")
```

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `area_km2` | Catchment area, used to turn millimetres into cubic metres per second |
| `calibration` | First and last date of the period the calibration is fitted to. Anything before it is warm-up: simulated, so the model's stores settle, but not scored |
| `validation` | A later period the calibration never sees, used to check the result honestly |
| `test` (optional) | A final period kept back until everything is decided, scored once |
| `config` (optional) | A model configuration file in the folder, if this catchment needs a different model |
| `thresholds`, `rating` (optional) | Warning thresholds to score; see [Scoring a simulation](scoring.html) |

# Before you start: how long will it take?

Time one model run, then multiply. A calibration of five parameters with three starting
points uses roughly 1,000 to 2,000 model runs.

```{r budget}
one_run <- system.time(
  for (i in 1:20) run_pdm(pdm_from_config(truths$B01), data.frame(rain = 0, pet = rep(0.05, n)))
)[["elapsed"]] / 20
c(seconds_per_run = signif(one_run, 2),
  estimated_minutes_for_8 = round(8 * 1500 * one_run / 60, 1))
```

For a real batch, measure on a few catchments first; see the pilot script in
[Calibration](calibration.html).

# Running the batch

Say who you are, then give the folder of catchments and a folder for the results. The rest
of the settings are the protocol, the same for every catchment: how many starting points,
how many steps each search may take, which parameters to leave alone.

```{r run-part}
options(pdmS7.user = "Ann Hydrologist", pdmS7.role = "custodian")
results <- file.path(tempdir(), "results")
protocol <- list(starts = 3, control = list(maxit = 25),
                 exclude = c("distribution.b", "groundwater.kb"))
part <- do.call(calibrate_batch, c(list(basins, results, only = c("B01", "B02", "B03")),
                                   protocol))
part
```

Suppose the computer was switched off at this point, after three catchments. Nothing is
lost: each catchment has its own project folder recording exactly how far it got. Run the
same command again, this time for all of them:

```{r run-all}
elapsed <- system.time(
  status <- do.call(calibrate_batch, c(list(basins, results), protocol))
)[["elapsed"]]
status
```

The three finished catchments took a moment each: the batch read their records, saw every
step already done, and moved on. The others ran in full. Each catchment's random starting
points come from its own name, so B01 gets the same result whether it runs alone or with a
hundred others.

## While it runs

On a long batch, open a second R session and look at progress at any time:

```{r status-anytime, eval=FALSE}
batch_status(results)
```

It reads `batch-status.csv` in the results folder, which records each catchment as
`queued`, `running`, `done` or `failed`.

## When a catchment fails

One catchment failed, and the batch carried on without it:

```{r failure}
status[state == "failed", .(basin, step, message)]
```

The message says what is wrong and the step says where it stopped: the data were refused
before anything was calibrated. Fix the file and run the batch again for just that
catchment:

```{r fix}
fixed <- data.table::fread(file.path(basins, "B06", "forcing.csv"))
fixed$pet <- abs(fixed$pet)
data.table::fwrite(fixed, file.path(basins, "B06", "forcing.csv"))
status <- do.call(calibrate_batch, c(list(basins, results, only = "B06"), protocol))
status
```

The failed attempt is still on record in B06's project, followed by the successful one.

## On a server

On a shared server, put the call in a script and start it so that it keeps running after
you log off. Use one core per catchment, up to what the server can spare:

```{r server, eval=FALSE}
# batch.R
library(pdmS7)
options(pdmS7.user = "Ann Hydrologist", pdmS7.role = "custodian")
calibrate_batch("basins", "results", starts = 20, cores = 32,
                owner = "Deputy Director", steward = "Sam Steward")
```

```sh
nohup Rscript batch.R > batch.log 2>&1 &
```

If the server is restarted, run the same command again.

# Reading the results

`batch_results()` gathers every catchment into one table, with the headline score (here NSE)
on the calibration and validation periods:

```{r results}
table <- batch_results(results)
table[, .(project, state, calibration = round(candidate_score, 3),
          validation = round(validation_score, 3))]
```

```{r scores, fig.cap="Left: each catchment's score on the calibration period against the validation period; points below the line did worse on data the calibration never saw. Right: the share of catchments reaching each validation score."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 1, 1))
lim <- range(c(table$candidate_score, table$validation_score))
plot(table$candidate_score, table$validation_score, pch = 16, col = pal[1], xlim = lim,
     ylim = lim, xlab = "Calibration NSE", ylab = "Validation NSE")
abline(0, 1, col = pal[7])
text(table$candidate_score, table$validation_score, table$project, pos = 4, cex = 0.7,
     col = pal[5])
plot(sort(table$validation_score), seq_len(nrow(table)) / nrow(table), type = "s", lwd = 2,
     col = pal[1], xlab = "Validation NSE", ylab = "Share of catchments", ylim = c(0, 1))
```

Report the whole spread, not just the average. The middle says how good the model usually
is; the worst few say where it fails, and those are the catchments to look at first.

## Did the search find the best answer?

Each calibration started from three different points. If they all ended at the same score,
the answer is probably the best there is. If they ended at different scores, the search
may have stopped in the wrong place.

```{r starts}
agreement <- do.call(rbind, lapply(table$project, function(id) {
  fit <- read_entry(file.path(results, id), 4)
  scores <- unlist(fit$start_results$objective)
  data.frame(basin = id, best = signif(min(scores), 3), worst = signif(max(scores), 3),
             finished = sum(unlist(fit$start_results$convergence) == 0))
}))
agreement$agree <- (agreement$worst - agreement$best) < 1e-3
agreement
```

`finished` counts the starts that ended because they could improve no further, rather than
because they ran out of steps. Where starts disagree but all finished, the catchment has
more than one "best" answer and needs more starting points. Where they ran out of steps, the
search simply needs longer; this example allows only 25 steps to keep it quick, and a real
batch should allow 200 or more.

## Did it find the truth?

Only possible here, because we made the catchments up: compare each fitted value with the
true one. The two surface time constants can swap places without changing the flow, so they
are compared as the faster and the slower of the pair.

```{r recovery, fig.cap="Fitted against true values, one point per catchment. Points on the line are exact."}
pairs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(table$project, function(id) {
  fitted <- read_entry(file.path(results, id), 4)$configuration
  value <- function(cfg) {
    k <- sort(c(cfg$surface$k1, cfg$surface$k2))
    c(fc = cfg$fc, cmax = cfg$distribution$cmax, kg = cfg$recharge$kg, k_fast = k[1],
      k_slow = k[2])
  }
  data.frame(basin = id, parameter = names(value(truths[[id]])), truth = value(truths[[id]]),
             fitted = value(fitted))
}))
par(mfrow = c(1, 5), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5), mgp = c(2.2, 0.7, 0))
for (p in unique(pairs$parameter)) {
  d <- pairs[pairs$parameter == p, ]
  lim <- range(c(d$truth, d$fitted))
  plot(d$truth, d$fitted, pch = 16, col = pal[1], xlim = lim, ylim = lim, main = p,
       xlab = "True", ylab = "Fitted", log = if (p == "kg") "xy" else "")
  abline(0, 1, col = pal[7])
}
```

```{r recovery-table}
pairs$error <- abs(pairs$fitted / pairs$truth - 1)
typical <- aggregate(cbind(typical_error = error) ~ parameter, data = pairs,
                     FUN = function(x) round(stats::median(x), 3))
typical
best <- typical$parameter[order(typical$typical_error)]
```

The typical error is the middle value across catchments, as a fraction: 0.01 means 1 per
cent out. Here `r best[1]` and `r best[2]` come back almost exactly: they control how much
water there is and how the river recedes, which every week of record shows. `r best[5]` and
`r best[4]` are the furthest out, typically about
`r round(100 * max(typical$typical_error))` per cent, partly because this example stops each
search after 25 steps, before most of them had finished. In other cases a parameter is badly
off even when the fit is excellent, because the data hold little information about it: the
size of a soil store that two autumn months never fill, for example.

The lesson for real catchments, where the truth is unknown: a good score does not prove the
parameters are right. Longer records, the parameter sensitivity plots in each catchment's
report, and [staged calibration](calibration.html) all help.

# Checking the work

Every catchment's record can be checked for tampering, and reviewed and signed off like any
other calibration (see [Logging a manual calibration](calibration-log.html)). Start the
review with the worst performers:

```{r verify}
folders <- file.path(results, table$project)
table(intact = vapply(folders, function(f) all(verify_project(f)$ok), logical(1)))
```

```{r reports, eval=FALSE}
worst <- table[order(validation_score)][1:5]
for (f in file.path(results, worst$project)) build_report(f)
```

```{r cleanup, include=FALSE}
options(pdmS7.user = NULL, pdmS7.role = NULL)
unlink(c(basins, results), recursive = TRUE)
```

# Summary

| Task | How |
|---|---|
| Prepare | One folder per catchment: `forcing.csv`, `flow.csv`, `basin.yml` |
| Estimate the time | Time one run; multiply by catchments, starts and about 1,500 runs per calibration |
| Run | `calibrate_batch(basins, results, starts = , cores = )` |
| Check progress | `batch_status(results)` from another session |
| After a crash or restart | Run the same command again |
| Fix a failure | Correct the data, then `calibrate_batch(..., only = "ID")` |
| Collect | `batch_results(results)` |
| Review | `verify_project()`, `build_report()` on the worst first, then sign off |

For many model structures in each catchment rather than one, see
[Choosing a model structure](choosing-structure.html).
